“POLITICIZATION IS PUSHING TROOPS TOWARD THE EXIT.” — A national survey of service members, veterans, and military families reveals that 53% of active-duty troops say increasing political interference and partisan polarization within the armed forces are driving them to leave service early—more than double the number citing pay or benefits.

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command, and you keep politics out of the mission. For too long, political leaders have treated the military as a partisan backdrop rather than protecting the core readiness of the force.”

— Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army Veteran & Executive Director of Common Defense

Key Findings from the National Survey
Politicization Outpaces Pay and Quality of Life: According to the latest national survey conducted by Common Defense, 53% of active-duty respondents report that growing political polarization makes them want to separate sooner, while only 5% say it encourages them to stay. By comparison, just 26% cited compensation and benefits as their primary retention concern.

Bipartisan Concern Across the Ranks: Frustration over politicization crosses traditional party affiliations. Among Republican-identifying service members and veterans, 72% agree that military families are being sidelined by political agendas, and 63% state defense policies are increasingly engineered for short-term domestic political gain.

Widespread Institutional Discontent: Over 79% of surveyed troops, veterans, and military dependents feel that civilian leadership and broader society are leaving the military community behind, with 74% expressing disapproval of how Congress oversees defense affairs.

Protecting the Apolitical Tradition: The survey highlighted strong opposition to using armed forces for domestic political functions: 55% of respondents reject deploying active-duty troops to monitor civilian polling stations or participate in domestic civil policing, reaffirming the constitutional standard of an apolitical military.

Strategic Implications for Retention & Readiness
Compounding the Recruiting Crisis: As all branches battle historically challenging recruiting environments, losing experienced mid-career NCOs and junior officers over political fatigue threatens institutional knowledge, unit cohesion, and technical combat capabilities.

Erosion of Public Trust: Decades of defense polling demonstrate that public confidence in the armed forces relies directly on its strictly non-partisan status. Partisan debates over command appointments, social messaging, and foreign policy rhetoric risk undermining that foundational trust.

Mission Focus vs. Narrative Battles: Frontline leaders emphasize that unit effectiveness hinges on warfighting competency, tactical drills, and equipment readiness, warning that culture-war distractions degrade morale in operational formations.

Honoring the memory and heroism of U.S. Marine Corporal Seamus M. Davey, an elite reconnaissance scout with 2d Force Reconnaissance Company (attached to 4th Force Recon Battalion).

On October 21, 2005, during combat operations in Abu Hyatt, Al Anbar Province, Iraq, Cpl. Davey's team entered an insurgent staging house and was ambushed at point-blank range—less than ten feet away—by four armed enemy fighters.

Struck by multiple rounds, Davey collapsed to the ground. Completely disregarding his mortal wounds and personal safety, he immediately brought his weapon to bear and opened continuous suppressive fire on the gunmen. His decisive, selfless actions drew the enemy's fire away from the doorway, allowing his fellow Marines to safely withdraw from the kill zone and survive. Davey continued to engage the enemy until he succumbed to his wounds, just three days before his 26th birthday.

For his extraordinary heroism, he was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal with Combat "V" and the Purple Heart.

"Swift, Silent, Deadly." Semper Fidelis, Corporal Davey. Your brothers will never forget.

When the Chinese struck at Chosin Reservoir in late November 1950, Colonel Homer Litzenberg's 7th Marines were holding the exposed northern flank at Yudam-ni — the first to take the blow and the last to pull back. His regiment fought through some of the worst winter combat in American history, much of it at night, much of it hand to hand.

Litzenberg had drilled his men relentlessly, and it showed: the 7th Marines held together when units around them were coming apart. He later said the real heroes were the nineteen-year-old riflemen who stood their ground in cold that froze weapons solid.

For Chosin he received the Navy Cross. He never bragged about it. The regiment's stand said everything.

In November 1950, Major General Oliver P. Smith's 1st Marine Division was strung out around the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea when some 120,000 Chinese troops closed in around them. It was fifty degrees below zero, the wounded were freezing in their sleeping bags, and every road out ran through the enemy.

Smith refused to panic. He built a rolling perimeter, brought up air support, and marched his division seventy miles through the Chinese lines to the sea at Hungnam — bringing out not just his men but the Army units trapped alongside them. Asked if this was a retreat, he gave the line that defined him: "Retreat, hell! We're just attacking in a different direction."

#OliverPSmith #ChosinReservoir #USMC #KoreanWar #NeverForget

The military classifies an incident as a Class A mishap when it results in a fatality, permanent total disability, the complete destruction of an aircraft, or damage exceeding $2.5 million.

The spike in major incidents has reignited fierce debate across the defense community regarding the root causes:

Relentless operational tempo and extended deployments wearing down crews

Severe maintenance backlogs, parts cannibalization, and shipyard delays

Retention shortfalls among experienced aviation mechanics and crew chiefs

Aging airframes pushed past their intended operational service life

When maintenance intervals are cut short and flight crews are stretched thin, the margin for error on a carrier flight deck shrinks to zero.

To our sailors, aviators, and maintainers: what is the biggest factor driving this spike in mishaps? Is it burnout, parts availability, or leadership pressure?

Two Women Shatter Precedent By Pushing Deep Into Navy SEAL BUD/S Pipeline
Two female candidates attempting to earn the coveted Navy SEAL trident have advanced further through the military's grueling selection pipeline than any women in history. According to investigative reporting from CBS News, an enlisted sailor and a commissioned naval officer entered Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL (BUD/S) training at Naval Amphibious Base Coronado in California, conquering the brutal initial conditioning weeks that eliminate nearly half of every class.

Key Historic Milestones
Historic Hell Week Milestone
The enlisted candidate broke all prior records by entering Hell Week, the punishing 5.5-day crucible that involves around 200 miles of running, freezing surf immersion, and barely four hours of total sleep, before being medically withdrawn.

Conquering The 45 Percent Drop Gate
Navy records compiled between 1998 and 2023 document that roughly 45 percent of all candidates voluntarily quit or get dropped during the three weeks preceding Hell Week, underscoring the exceptional endurance required to reach week four.

Naval Officer Performance
The female naval officer advanced into the third week of Phase 1 before being rolled back to a subsequent training class and subsequently requesting a voluntary drop prior to Hell Week.

Naval Special Warfare Precedent
While no woman has completed SEAL qualification since combat exclusions were lifted in 2016, Naval Special Warfare previously saw its first female graduate in 2021 when a sailor successfully completed the rigorous pipeline to become a Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewman (SWCC).

Petty Officer Second Class Matthew Gene “Axe” Axelson was just 29 years old and married for two years when a reconnaissance mission in the rugged Hindu Kush mountains of Kunar Province, Afghanistan, took his life on June 28, 2005.

Inserted on a high-stakes mission during Operation Red Wings alongside Lt. Michael P. Murphy, Danny Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell, the four-man reconnaissance team was compromised and rapidly surrounded by a heavily armed insurgent force holding the high ground.

 Despite suffering multiple grievous gunshot wounds in the chaotic firefight, Axelson refused to fall back or yield. According to his official Navy Cross citation, he urged his closest teammate to escape while he continued engaging enemy fighters, providing covering fire until he was mortally wounded.

The brutal engagement ultimately claimed the lives of Axelson, Murphy, and Dietz, along with 16 special operators and aviators aboard the downed MH-47 rescue helicopter leaving Luttrell as the sole survivor of the initial team. Axelson was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his extraordinary heroism and selfless devotion to his brothers-in-arms.

Engineered at the legendary Skunk Works facility for NASA’s Quesst mission, the nearly 100-foot-long experimental aircraft is built to solve one of aviation’s oldest hurdles. Its radical layout features an elongated 30-foot needle nose and an engine mounted directly atop the fuselage, geometry shaped to disperse supersonic shockwaves before they can merge into a window-rattling sonic boom. Because the elongated nose completely blocks forward cockpit sightlines, test pilots fly without a forward windshield, relying instead on NASA’s eXternal Vision System to stream a real-time 4K camera feed of the airspace onto an interior display.

Cruising at Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet, the aircraft softens the traditional sonic boom into a gentle acoustic thump on the ground. NASA plans to use flight-test acoustics from overland runs to provide data to regulators and potentially lift the decades-old ban on commercial overland supersonic flight.

OVER AN HOUR IN 15-FOOT SWELLS. A MASTER EOD TECHNICIAN SAVED FIVE DROWNING AIRMEN IN A RAGING SEA.

Explosive Ordnance Disposal technicians are trained to defuse bombs under extreme pressure, but true courage does not stop at the bomb suit.

While stationed in Turkey, Senior Master Sergeant Riemer was on a morale boat trip in the Aegean Sea when a sudden, violent storm erupted. Gale-force winds and churning 15-foot swells pushed the vessel away from a group of airmen who were swimming toward a nearby island, leaving them stranded in open water.

Seeing panic set in, Riemer plunged off the deck into the maelstrom. In near-zero visibility, he fought relentless currents for thirty grueling minutes to pull two drowning airmen back to the boat. Looking across the churning water, he spotted three more airmen clinging to each other as their strength failed. Disregarding his own exhaustion, Riemer grabbed flotation devices and dove into the raging waves a second time, secured a safety line around the trio, and hauled all three aboard.

Over an hour in the water, Riemer single-handedly pulled five lives from the sea. When asked about his thoughts during the chaos, he calmly said, “I was thinking I’m an EOD technician, and EOD technicians solve complex problems.”

According to official reporting from DVIDS, Riemer was presented with the Airman's Medal for his heroic actions.

A combat-tested leader who holds the distinction of being the first EOD technician in military history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Senior Master Sgt. Riemer proved that the warrior mindset shows up whenever lives are on the line.

On August 5, 1964, Lieutenant Everett Alvarez's A-4 went down over North Vietnam — making him the first American naval aviator captured in the Vietnam War. He was twenty-six years old. He would not see freedom for eight and a half years.

Alvarez endured some of the longest continuous captivity of any American POW: years of isolation, torture, and uncertainty in camps across North Vietnam. He resisted, he survived, and he came home in 1973 with his dignity intact.

The war lasted a decade for America. For Everett Alvarez, it lasted 3,113 days — and he never gave his captors what they wanted most: his spirit.

“SHOT IN THE HELMET AND ARM, HE RIGGED WEBBING TO LOWER FOUR PARALYZED TEAMMATES DOWN A 60-FOOT CLIFF.”

On April 6, 2008, during the Battle of Shok Valley in the rugged Nuristan Province of Afghanistan, Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336, 3rd Special Forces Group) walked into an ambush of catastrophic proportions.

Over 200 entrenched enemy fighters held the high ground on terraced cliffs, raining down relentless machine-gun, sniper, and RPG fire. The assault element was trapped on a narrow, 100-foot ridge, taking catastrophic casualties.

Down at the base of the mountain, Special Forces Medical Sergeant Ronald J. Shurer II didn’t hesitate. Under heavy fire, he charged up the steep, snow-covered rocky incline to reach his pinned-down teammates.

What followed across the next six hours stands as one of the greatest feats of combat medicine in American military history:

 While treating a critically wounded commando, an enemy sniper round struck the back of Shurer’s helmet with concussive force. He shook off the impact and continued treating casualties until another bullet struck his arm. Ignoring his own wounds, he refused to stop.

Shurer stabilized multiple Green Berets and Afghan Commandos who had suffered catastrophic trauma, including severed limbs, traumatic brain injuries, and paralysis, all while exposed on the sheer face of the mountain.

Facing imminent encirclement, Shurer rigged nylon tubular webbing around rocks and trees. Under direct enemy fire, he manually lowered four paralyzed and critically injured teammates down a 60-foot near-vertical cliff, using his own body as a physical shield to deflect incoming rounds and falling rock debris.

Shurer then helped carry the wounded across a freezing, raging river to the medevac landing zone, continuing to treat patients until every man was evacuated. Because of his actions, not a single American died on that mountain.

President Donald J. Trump presented Ronald J. Shurer II with the Medal of Honor on October 1, 2018.

After leaving the Army, Shurer continued his service to the nation as a Special Agent on the U.S. Secret Service Counter Assault Team (CAT). In May 2020, he tragically passed away from stage 4 lung cancer at the age of 41, leaving behind his wife Miranda and two young sons.

A true Green Beret. A warrior medic. An American hero.

On October 26, 1967, Lieutenant Commander John McCain's A-4 was shot down over Hanoi. He ejected with two broken arms and a shattered leg, was bayoneted by his captors, and spent the next five and a half years as a POW in the infamous "Hanoi Hilton."

When the North Vietnamese discovered his father was an admiral, they offered him early release — a propaganda prize. McCain refused, honoring the POW code: first in, first out. He endured years more of torture rather than leave his fellow prisoners behind.

He came home in 1973 and served his country for the rest of his life. But it was in that cell, refusing to break, that John McCain showed who he was.

HISTORY IN THE PACIFIC: The U.S. Navy has deployed its first operational drone warship alongside a Carrier Strike Group.

In a major milestone for naval warfare, the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group got underway in the Pacific accompanied by the Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel (MUSV) Seahawk—marking the first time an autonomous robotic warship has deployed operationally with a frontline carrier strike force.

What this means for the fleet:

• The Platform: Seahawk is a 145-ton trimaran drone ship engineered to navigate open ocean autonomously for months at a time, requiring zero crew aboard.

• The Mission: Operating miles ahead of the strike group, autonomous surface vessels act as forward radar pickets, electronic warfare nodes, and anti-submarine tracking scouts—detecting threats long before they enter missile range of the carrier.

• The Pacific Strategy: As peer threats expand long-range anti-ship missile arsenals across the Indo-Pacific, pairing manned supercarriers and destroyers with expendable, sensor-packed unmanned vessels is the Navy's primary answer to distributed maritime operations.

Seeing sailors watch a robotic warship trail off the fantail is a surreal glimpse into the future of naval combat.

Would you trust autonomous drone ships to hold the line in a high-intensity naval fight, or does human instinct on the bridge remain irreplaceable?

“BY 2030, POLAND WILL FIELD MORE TANKS THAN GERMANY, FRANCE, ITALY, AND BRITAIN COMBINED.”

While much of Western Europe spent the post-Cold War decades downsizing heavy armor divisions, Poland a nation of 38 million is executing the most ambitious conventional military buildup on the European continent.

By the end of the decade, the Polish Land Forces are projected to field an active arsenal of over 1,500 modern main battle tanks. For comparison, the combined tank fleets of the United Kingdom (~150), France (~220), Germany (~300), and Italy (~200) total fewer than 900 vehicles.

Key pillars behind Poland’s armored juggernaut:

Warsaw has acquired 366 U.S. Abrams tanks, including 250 factory-fresh M1A2 SEPv3 variants and 116 upgraded M1A1 FEP models to anchor heavy mechanized divisions along the eastern border.

A landmark agreement secures 1,000 K2 Black Panther tanks, consisting of 180 initial deliveries and 820 K2PL variants co-produced in Polish factories with localized reactive armor and active protection systems.

 Poland leads the entire NATO alliance in defense investment, dedicating over 4% of its GDP to military procurement and readiness.

The tank buildup is integrated with 96 Boeing AH-64E Apache Guardian attack helicopters, hundreds of HIMARS and K239 Chunmoo rocket launchers, and F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters.

 Poland is actively scaling its armed forces toward a target of 300,000 personnel, cementing its status as NATO’s primary conventional land bulwark on the Eastern Flank.

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

“POLITICIZATION IS PUSHING TROOPS TOWARD THE EXIT.” — A national survey of service members, veterans, and military families reveals that 53% of active-duty troops say increasing political interference and partisan polarization within the armed forces are driving them to leave service early—more than double the number citing pay or benefits.

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command, and you keep politics out of the mission. For too long, political leaders have treated the military as a partisan backdrop rather than protecting the core readiness of the force.”

— Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army Veteran & Executive Director of Common Defense

Key Findings from the National Survey
Politicization Outpaces Pay and Quality of Life: According to the latest national survey conducted by Common Defense, 53% of active-duty respondents report that growing political polarization makes them want to separate sooner, while only 5% say it encourages them to stay. By comparison, just 26% cited compensation and benefits as their primary retention concern.

Bipartisan Concern Across the Ranks: Frustration over politicization crosses traditional party affiliations. Among Republican-identifying service members and veterans, 72% agree that military families are being sidelined by political agendas, and 63% state defense policies are increasingly engineered for short-term domestic political gain.

Widespread Institutional Discontent: Over 79% of surveyed troops, veterans, and military dependents feel that civilian leadership and broader society are leaving the military community behind, with 74% expressing disapproval of how Congress oversees defense affairs.

Protecting the Apolitical Tradition: The survey highlighted strong opposition to using armed forces for domestic political functions: 55% of respondents reject deploying active-duty troops to monitor civilian polling stations or participate in domestic civil policing, reaffirming the constitutional standard of an apolitical military.

Strategic Implications for Retention & Readiness
Compounding the Recruiting Crisis: As all branches battle historically challenging recruiting environments, losing experienced mid-career NCOs and junior officers over political fatigue threatens institutional knowledge, unit cohesion, and technical combat capabilities.

Erosion of Public Trust: Decades of defense polling demonstrate that public confidence in the armed forces relies directly on its strictly non-partisan status. Partisan debates over command appointments, social messaging, and foreign policy rhetoric risk undermining that foundational trust.

Mission Focus vs. Narrative Battles: Frontline leaders emphasize that unit effectiveness hinges on warfighting competency, tactical drills, and equipment readiness, warning that culture-war distractions degrade morale in operational formations.

Honoring the memory and heroism of U.S. Marine Corporal Seamus M. Davey, an elite reconnaissance scout with 2d Force Reconnaissance Company (attached to 4th Force Recon Battalion).

On October 21, 2005, during combat operations in Abu Hyatt, Al Anbar Province, Iraq, Cpl. Davey's team entered an insurgent staging house and was ambushed at point-blank range—less than ten feet away—by four armed enemy fighters.

Struck by multiple rounds, Davey collapsed to the ground. Completely disregarding his mortal wounds and personal safety, he immediately brought his weapon to bear and opened continuous suppressive fire on the gunmen. His decisive, selfless actions drew the enemy's fire away from the doorway, allowing his fellow Marines to safely withdraw from the kill zone and survive. Davey continued to engage the enemy until he succumbed to his wounds, just three days before his 26th birthday.

For his extraordinary heroism, he was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal with Combat "V" and the Purple Heart.

"Swift, Silent, Deadly." Semper Fidelis, Corporal Davey. Your brothers will never forget.

When the Chinese struck at Chosin Reservoir in late November 1950, Colonel Homer Litzenberg's 7th Marines were holding the exposed northern flank at Yudam-ni — the first to take the blow and the last to pull back. His regiment fought through some of the worst winter combat in American history, much of it at night, much of it hand to hand.

Litzenberg had drilled his men relentlessly, and it showed: the 7th Marines held together when units around them were coming apart. He later said the real heroes were the nineteen-year-old riflemen who stood their ground in cold that froze weapons solid.

For Chosin he received the Navy Cross. He never bragged about it. The regiment's stand said everything.

#HomerLitzenberg #ChosinReservoir #USMC #KoreanWar #NeverForget

In November 1950, Major General Oliver P. Smith's 1st Marine Division was strung out around the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea when some 120,000 Chinese troops closed in around them. It was fifty degrees below zero, the wounded were freezing in their sleeping bags, and every road out ran through the enemy.

Smith refused to panic. He built a rolling perimeter, brought up air support, and marched his division seventy miles through the Chinese lines to the sea at Hungnam — bringing out not just his men but the Army units trapped alongside them. Asked if this was a retreat, he gave the line that defined him: "Retreat, hell! We're just attacking in a different direction."

#OliverPSmith #ChosinReservoir #USMC #KoreanWar #NeverForget

BREAKING: The U.S. Navy has recorded a decade-high spike in catastrophic accidents, reporting 16 Class A aviation mishaps and 11 serious afloat incidents in fiscal year 2026—the highest total since 2014.

The military classifies an incident as a Class A mishap when it results in a fatality, permanent total disability, the complete destruction of an aircraft, or damage exceeding $2.5 million.

Over the past 12 months, carrier strike groups and naval aviation squadrons have faced unrelenting operational pressure—ranging from sustained combat engagements in the Red Sea to high-tempo deterrence patrols across the Indo-Pacific and Mediterranean.

The spike in major incidents has reignited fierce debate across the defense community regarding the root causes:

Relentless operational tempo and extended deployments wearing down crews

Severe maintenance backlogs, parts cannibalization, and shipyard delays

Retention shortfalls among experienced aviation mechanics and crew chiefs

Aging airframes pushed past their intended operational service life

When maintenance intervals are cut short and flight crews are stretched thin, the margin for error on a carrier flight deck shrinks to zero.

To our sailors, aviators, and maintainers: what is the biggest factor driving this spike in mishaps? Is it burnout, parts availability, or leadership pressure?

Brigadier General Anna Mae Hays led the Army Nurse Corps through the Vietnam War — and on June 11, 1970, she became the first woman in American history to wear a general's stars. No woman in any American armed service had ever held general rank before.

Hays had served in World War II, Korea, and Vietnam, building the nursing force that kept the Army's medical system running through three wars. She fought for her nurses' recognition, their working conditions, and their place in a military that wasn't built for them.

She didn't just break the glass ceiling. She did it in uniform, while running a war's worth of hospitals — and she held the door open for every woman who followed.

Two Women Shatter Precedent By Pushing Deep Into Navy SEAL BUD/S Pipeline
Two female candidates attempting to earn the coveted Navy SEAL trident have advanced further through the military's grueling selection pipeline than any women in history. According to investigative reporting from CBS News, an enlisted sailor and a commissioned naval officer entered Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL (BUD/S) training at Naval Amphibious Base Coronado in California, conquering the brutal initial conditioning weeks that eliminate nearly half of every class.

Key Historic Milestones
Historic Hell Week Milestone
The enlisted candidate broke all prior records by entering Hell Week, the punishing 5.5-day crucible that involves around 200 miles of running, freezing surf immersion, and barely four hours of total sleep, before being medically withdrawn.

Conquering The 45 Percent Drop Gate
Navy records compiled between 1998 and 2023 document that roughly 45 percent of all candidates voluntarily quit or get dropped during the three weeks preceding Hell Week, underscoring the exceptional endurance required to reach week four.

Naval Officer Performance
The female naval officer advanced into the third week of Phase 1 before being rolled back to a subsequent training class and subsequently requesting a voluntary drop prior to Hell Week.

Naval Special Warfare Precedent
While no woman has completed SEAL qualification since combat exclusions were lifted in 2016, Naval Special Warfare previously saw its first female graduate in 2021 when a sailor successfully completed the rigorous pipeline to become a Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewman (SWCC).

What does true brotherhood look like when surviving seems impossible, yet you choose to keep firing so your teammate has a chance to live?

Petty Officer Second Class Matthew Gene “Axe” Axelson was just 29 years old and married for two years when a reconnaissance mission in the rugged Hindu Kush mountains of Kunar Province, Afghanistan, took his life on June 28, 2005.

Inserted on a high-stakes mission during Operation Red Wings alongside Lt. Michael P. Murphy, Danny Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell, the four-man reconnaissance team was compromised and rapidly surrounded by a heavily armed insurgent force holding the high ground.

 Despite suffering multiple grievous gunshot wounds in the chaotic firefight, Axelson refused to fall back or yield. According to his official Navy Cross citation, he urged his closest teammate to escape while he continued engaging enemy fighters, providing covering fire until he was mortally wounded.

The brutal engagement ultimately claimed the lives of Axelson, Murphy, and Dietz, along with 16 special operators and aviators aboard the downed MH-47 rescue helicopter leaving Luttrell as the sole survivor of the initial team. Axelson was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his extraordinary heroism and selfless devotion to his brothers-in-arms.

Engineered at the legendary Skunk Works facility for NASA’s Quesst mission, the nearly 100-foot-long experimental aircraft is built to solve one of aviation’s oldest hurdles. Its radical layout features an elongated 30-foot needle nose and an engine mounted directly atop the fuselage, geometry shaped to disperse supersonic shockwaves before they can merge into a window-rattling sonic boom. Because the elongated nose completely blocks forward cockpit sightlines, test pilots fly without a forward windshield, relying instead on NASA’s eXternal Vision System to stream a real-time 4K camera feed of the airspace onto an interior display.

Cruising at Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet, the aircraft softens the traditional sonic boom into a gentle acoustic thump on the ground. NASA plans to use flight-test acoustics from overland runs to provide data to regulators and potentially lift the decades-old ban on commercial overland supersonic flight.

OVER AN HOUR IN 15-FOOT SWELLS. A MASTER EOD TECHNICIAN SAVED FIVE DROWNING AIRMEN IN A RAGING SEA.

Explosive Ordnance Disposal technicians are trained to defuse bombs under extreme pressure, but true courage does not stop at the bomb suit.

While stationed in Turkey, Senior Master Sergeant Riemer was on a morale boat trip in the Aegean Sea when a sudden, violent storm erupted. Gale-force winds and churning 15-foot swells pushed the vessel away from a group of airmen who were swimming toward a nearby island, leaving them stranded in open water.

Seeing panic set in, Riemer plunged off the deck into the maelstrom. In near-zero visibility, he fought relentless currents for thirty grueling minutes to pull two drowning airmen back to the boat. Looking across the churning water, he spotted three more airmen clinging to each other as their strength failed. Disregarding his own exhaustion, Riemer grabbed flotation devices and dove into the raging waves a second time, secured a safety line around the trio, and hauled all three aboard.

Over an hour in the water, Riemer single-handedly pulled five lives from the sea. When asked about his thoughts during the chaos, he calmly said, “I was thinking I’m an EOD technician, and EOD technicians solve complex problems.”

According to official reporting from DVIDS, Riemer was presented with the Airman's Medal for his heroic actions.

A combat-tested leader who holds the distinction of being the first EOD technician in military history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Senior Master Sgt. Riemer proved that the warrior mindset shows up whenever lives are on the line.

On August 5, 1964, Lieutenant Everett Alvarez's A-4 went down over North Vietnam — making him the first American naval aviator captured in the Vietnam War. He was twenty-six years old. He would not see freedom for eight and a half years.

Alvarez endured some of the longest continuous captivity of any American POW: years of isolation, torture, and uncertainty in camps across North Vietnam. He resisted, he survived, and he came home in 1973 with his dignity intact.

The war lasted a decade for America. For Everett Alvarez, it lasted 3,113 days — and he never gave his captors what they wanted most: his spirit.

#EverettAlvarez #POW #VietnamWar #USNavy #NeverForget

(5/18/2012) – Corporal Christopher B. Farias, 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment, was awarded the nation’s second highest award for bravery during a ceremony here, May 18.

Under Secretary of the Navy Robert Work presented the Navy Cross to Farias for heroic actions while serving as an assistant squad leader in the Kajaki district of Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2010.

After Farias, a native of La Porte, Texas, arrived in Afghanistan, the commanding officer pulled the Marines together and mentioned they would protect the Kajaki Dam and relieve British forces at the front line.

“To find out that we’re surrounded in three different areas by Taliban fighters, that’s telling me that we’re definitely on our own on this one,” Farias explained.

Farias was excited to do infantry missions because he had experience in Iraq with foot patrols and security and felt the Marines in his squad were well trained and confident in their abilities to complete their mission on the northern frontier of the Marines’ battlespace in Kajaki.

During the night of the fight, Farias requested to go on the mission because he enjoyed patrolling, he said. The Marines planned to set up an ambush against enemy forces moving throughout the area.

While preparing for the attack, the Marines received reports that enemy fighters called for reinforcements, including a “special weapon,” a 73-millimeter recoilless rifle. The rounds are larger than the rounds of some mortar systems.

Farias and the squad heard an explosion and received enemy fire from three positions in a vicious ambush. Several Marines lay wounded by the recoilless rifle, and insurgent forces adjusted their fires and continued to shoot into the Marines’ position.

“These guys were tactically and strategically smart,” said Farias. They were well-trained. To have guys who can fight just like you... they know how to maneuver, they know how to set you up for a proper ambush... to fight an enemy like that, it’s pretty insane.”

Farias suffered a concussion and fragmentation wounds in the neck and shoulder and received hasty treatment for his wounds before directing medical care for the other Marines. After securing the wounded, Farias climbed to a rooftop and controlled the fire of the machine guns to suppress enemy positions.

The suppressive fires kept the enemy down and allowed the squad to treat the wounded, clear a landing zone, and evacuate the casualties. Farias remained with his squad until an airstrike ended the engagement.

Afterward, Farias walked more than 2,000 meters back to a ground evacuation site. His neck was bleeding, and he felt drained due to blood loss; he remembered.

“As we were walking back, that’s when I started feeling every bit of pain possible,” recounted Farias. “I ended up realizing my right arm would not move. I could not move it to save my life if I wanted to.”

Farias was recommended for a Silver Star, which was upgraded to a Navy Cross. The Marines of 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment formed on the parade deck with M777 lightweight howitzers on display. Farias said he was honored to receive the award on behalf of his Marines and the unit.

“I don’t see it as actually for me,” Farias said. “I see it as for India Battery, but for me to stand there and be a representation for India Battery for that award... it’s a shocker.”

“SHOT IN THE HELMET AND ARM, HE RIGGED WEBBING TO LOWER FOUR PARALYZED TEAMMATES DOWN A 60-FOOT CLIFF.”

On April 6, 2008, during the Battle of Shok Valley in the rugged Nuristan Province of Afghanistan, Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336, 3rd Special Forces Group) walked into an ambush of catastrophic proportions.

Over 200 entrenched enemy fighters held the high ground on terraced cliffs, raining down relentless machine-gun, sniper, and RPG fire. The assault element was trapped on a narrow, 100-foot ridge, taking catastrophic casualties.

Down at the base of the mountain, Special Forces Medical Sergeant Ronald J. Shurer II didn’t hesitate. Under heavy fire, he charged up the steep, snow-covered rocky incline to reach his pinned-down teammates.

What followed across the next six hours stands as one of the greatest feats of combat medicine in American military history:

 While treating a critically wounded commando, an enemy sniper round struck the back of Shurer’s helmet with concussive force. He shook off the impact and continued treating casualties until another bullet struck his arm. Ignoring his own wounds, he refused to stop.

Shurer stabilized multiple Green Berets and Afghan Commandos who had suffered catastrophic trauma, including severed limbs, traumatic brain injuries, and paralysis, all while exposed on the sheer face of the mountain.

Facing imminent encirclement, Shurer rigged nylon tubular webbing around rocks and trees. Under direct enemy fire, he manually lowered four paralyzed and critically injured teammates down a 60-foot near-vertical cliff, using his own body as a physical shield to deflect incoming rounds and falling rock debris.

Shurer then helped carry the wounded across a freezing, raging river to the medevac landing zone, continuing to treat patients until every man was evacuated. Because of his actions, not a single American died on that mountain.

President Donald J. Trump presented Ronald J. Shurer II with the Medal of Honor on October 1, 2018.

After leaving the Army, Shurer continued his service to the nation as a Special Agent on the U.S. Secret Service Counter Assault Team (CAT). In May 2020, he tragically passed away from stage 4 lung cancer at the age of 41, leaving behind his wife Miranda and two young sons.

A true Green Beret. A warrior medic. An American hero.

On October 26, 1967, Lieutenant Commander John McCain's A-4 was shot down over Hanoi. He ejected with two broken arms and a shattered leg, was bayoneted by his captors, and spent the next five and a half years as a POW in the infamous "Hanoi Hilton."

When the North Vietnamese discovered his father was an admiral, they offered him early release — a propaganda prize. McCain refused, honoring the POW code: first in, first out. He endured years more of torture rather than leave his fellow prisoners behind.

He came home in 1973 and served his country for the rest of his life. But it was in that cell, refusing to break, that John McCain showed who he was.

Daniel "Chappie" James began as a Tuskegee Airman, flying P-51s in the last months of World War II. He kept climbing — through Korea, through Vietnam, where he commanded air power as deputy commander of 7th Air Force — until, in 1975, he became the first Black four-star general in American history.

James was as famous for his words as his wings: a fierce, eloquent patriot who believed in America enough to demand it live up to itself. In Vietnam, his leadership helped shape the air campaign; at home, his example helped shape the nation.

From Tuskegee to four stars — a journey measured not just in rank, but in the doors he opened behind him.

U.S. Army Major Robert Eldridge enlisted in December, 1986, joining the Special Forces Reserves.

"My father was in special forces and I knew quite a few people in Special Forces. I liked it. It sounded like what I wanted to do, so I pursued it," he said.

In 1997 he was commissioned as an infantry officer, where he served briefly before rejoining Special Forces as an officer as well.

In November of 2004 Eldridge deployed to Afghanistan for what should have been a deployment that lasted many months. But on Dec. 17, 2004 while conducting a patrol, Eldridge's vehicle, which was leading the patrol, hit an Improvised Explosive Device.

Eldridge was seriously injured, but the medic on his team, who had been driving the vehicle was able to begin treating him just minutes after the explosion. And within 30 minutes was been evacuated by a Blackhawk, he said.

Eldridge's leg had to be amputated as a result of the injuries, and he spent six months recovering in Walter Reed Medical Center.

Though Eldridge had the option to retire after his injury, he fought to stay in the Army.

"I could have medically retired but I fought to stay in," he said.

The benefits of being in Special Operations, he said, was the support he received from other Special Operations Soldiers up and down the chain of command, who visited him when he was in the hospital in Afghanistan and at Walter Reed.

"I wanted to go back," he said, "and my group commander and battalion supported my coming back."

They were following his recovery, making sure he was ok, and seeing if he wanted to stay in or not. In particular, he said, he benefitted from a Special Operations wounded warrior program called the Care Coalition.

Eldridge also had the support of his family throughout his recovery and decision to stay in the Army. They met him when he arrived at Walter Reed on December 19, 2004, he said.

Eldridge's family "absolutely" supported his going back to Special Operations, he said.

"When I showed up I told them I was going back to my unit, and they thoroughly supported me through the entire process, he said.

Eldridge redeployed to Afghanistan in March of 2007.

"Within a month and a half of getting back to my unit, I started conducting airborne operations again," he said.

He said, "it was a good deployment. I got to stay the whole time."

Eldridge earned a Bronze Star with ‘Valor' and a Purple Heart for the events of December 17, 2004.

HISTORY IN THE PACIFIC: The U.S. Navy has deployed its first operational drone warship alongside a Carrier Strike Group.

In a major milestone for naval warfare, the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group got underway in the Pacific accompanied by the Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel (MUSV) Seahawk—marking the first time an autonomous robotic warship has deployed operationally with a frontline carrier strike force.

What this means for the fleet:

• The Platform: Seahawk is a 145-ton trimaran drone ship engineered to navigate open ocean autonomously for months at a time, requiring zero crew aboard.

• The Mission: Operating miles ahead of the strike group, autonomous surface vessels act as forward radar pickets, electronic warfare nodes, and anti-submarine tracking scouts—detecting threats long before they enter missile range of the carrier.

• The Pacific Strategy: As peer threats expand long-range anti-ship missile arsenals across the Indo-Pacific, pairing manned supercarriers and destroyers with expendable, sensor-packed unmanned vessels is the Navy's primary answer to distributed maritime operations.

Seeing sailors watch a robotic warship trail off the fantail is a surreal glimpse into the future of naval combat.

Would you trust autonomous drone ships to hold the line in a high-intensity naval fight, or does human instinct on the bridge remain irreplaceable?

On the morning of September 11, 2001, Lieutenant Colonel Marilyn Wills stopped by her office to grab a sweater on her way to a meeting on the second floor of the Pentagon. As she sat in the meeting with civilians and other military personnel, American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the building near the conference room.

The explosion blew Wills across the room and lit her hair on fire. Sprinklers began to battle the flames, but a blinding smoke filled the room. Wills grabbed her sweater, now saturated from the sprinklers, and started crawling, hoping to find a door. Someone grabbed her ankle. Wills told the older civilian woman to stay close.

They both sucked on the fibers of her sweater for moisture and inhaled through it to help breathe in the smoke. Another woman joined them as they crawled away from the conference room. Wills continued encouraging them onward and shoving her sweater over their faces as they moved. One of the women disappeared as they moved toward a stream of light coming from a nearby window.

Wills helped another soldier break open the window as he hurled a fax machine through it, then stayed inside and helped lower others down from the second story window. She turned back to look for the woman who had disappeared, but was ordered to get out by a superior officer.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Despite her injuries and excessive smoke inhalation, Wills miraculously survived. For her heroism helping lead others stranded in the building to safety, Wills was awarded the Soldier's Medal.

Here’s what AURA farming really is .

Staff Sgt. Zachary J. Rhyner, Air Force Cross Recipient

March 2009: An Air Force Special Operations Command Air Commando saved lives in Afghanistan on April 6 during a lengthy battle by calling in air strikes to protect his team.

Staff Sgt. Zachary J. Rhyner, a special tactics combat controller assigned to the 21st Special Tactics Squadron at Pope Air Force Base, N.C., was deployed to Operation Enduring Freedom as the primary joint terminal attack controller while attached to a special forces team.

Then, a Senior Airman, Sergeant Rhyner, was part of a 100+-man combined assault force whose mission was to enter Shok Valley and capture a high-value target who was funding the insurgency. Sergeant Rhyner is credited with saving the 100-man team from being overrun twice in a six-and-a-half-hour battle.

Air Force Capt. Stewart Parker, the special forces commander at Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, was the command-and-control link to the JTACs on the ground as they entered Shok Valley.

“This was the first time U.S. special operations forces entered the territory,” said Captain Parker. “These were extraordinary conditions and the situation was dynamic.”

Shok Valley is located below 60-foot cliffs. The mission objective was at the top of the mountains surrounding the valley.

“Initial infiltration began that day with snow on the ground, jagged rocks, a fast-moving river and a cliff,” said Sergeant Rhyner. “There was a 5-foot wall you had to pull yourself up. The ridgeline trail was out of control.”

The expectation was to encounter fire from about 70 insurgents. One Air Force JTAC-qualified combat controller was attached to each team to call in air strikes, if needed.

“We were caught off guard as 200 enemy fighters approached,” said Air Force Staff Sgt. Rob Gutierrez, a combat controller with the second team in the fight. “Within 10 minutes, we were ambushed with heavy fire from 50 meters. The teams were split by a river 100 to 200 meters apart, north to south.”

Sergeant Rhyner was in charge of coordinating the air assets.

“I have never seen a situation this bad,” said Captain Parker, who was monitoring the situation back at the base. “The intel said the enemy was 40 feet away from Zach and his team at one point. It was dangerous.”

Within the first 15 minutes of fire, Sergeant Rhyner was wounded along with three team members.

“I was pulling security when I got shot in the leg,” he said. “The rounds hit my left thigh and went through my leg and hit another guy in the foot.”

He immediately felt pain and adrenalin.

“There was nowhere to go. I grabbed the wounded guys, but we were trapped by the enemy,” he said. “I was calling in air strikes and firing while moving the wounded down [the cliff].”

Sergeant Gutierrez could see insurgent fire coming from the buildings on the hilltops above them and was trying to get across the river to meet up with Sergeant Rhyner.

“Zach and I were in constant radio contact,” he said. “I could hear the ammunition, sniper fire and rocket-propelled grenades with multiple blasts. We tried to push to the north to collocate with Zach’s team, but every time we pushed up river, it put us in an open line of fire.”

“My team ran across the freezing river. The water came off the mountains and we were 100 to 200 feet beneath the enemy, like fish in a barrel,” said Sergeant Gutierrez.

As the enemy surrounded them, Sergeant Rhyner, who was being treated for his injuries by Capt. Kyle Walton, the special forces team leader, directed multiple rockets and gun runs from AH-64 helicopters against enemy positions.

“Zach was coordinating tremendous amounts of fire on both villages simultaneously,” said Sergeant Gutierrez. “Zach was in charge of the air strikes, since he was closest to the fight and could see even what the F-15 pilots could not.”

Forty-five minutes to an hour had gone by since the fight began.

“We were pinned down and I could see the enemy all over the hills running around,” said Sergeant Gutierrez. There were no stable targets. I kept the Apaches and the Hellfire missiles pressed to the north.”

Accurate sniper, machine gun and rocket-propelled grenade fire poured down on the assault force in a complex ambush initiated simultaneously from all directions as the team ascented the near-vertical terrain. He called in more than 50 close air strikes and strafing runs.

Staff Sgt. Zachary Rhyner deployed to Afghanistan in 2008. Sergeant Rhyner, a combat controller with the 21st Special Tactics Squadron, will be awarded the Air Force Cross Mar. 10, 2009 for his actions in Shok Valley, Afghanistan April 6, 2008.

Three hours into the fight, Sergeant Gutierrez reached Sergeant Rhyner’s position.

“Sergeant Gutierrez and I met on the cliff during the battle briefly. We shared a laugh, but it was a busy, bleak situation,” Sergeant Rhyner said.

Sergeant Rhyner had been calling in air strikes for three hours while he was injured, however he still felt responsible for the others who had been hurt. With disregard for his own life, he tried to get the injured to safety, still in the open line of fire.

“I left injured personnel in a house and I had to get over there,” he said. “I was frustrated being wounded. I tried to get the bombs there fast and talk to the pilots who didn’t see what I saw on the ground.”

Five or six hours into the fight, as it was getting dark, intelligence informed the JTACs that enemy reinforcements were 10 kilometers away carrying enemy rockets and missiles.

“We continued to fight our way up the hill and the [helicopters] came,” said Sergeant Gutierrez. “Zach was talking to the helos and gave the coordinates to lay the bombs on the village, while I kept the A-10s and the Apaches out of the way.”

Sergeant Rhyner called in a total of 4,570 rounds of cannon fire, nine Hellfire missiles, 162 rockets, 12 500-pound bombs and one 2,000-pound bomb, constantly engaging the enemy with his M-4 rifle to deter their advance.

“Zach acted fast and shut down the fighting,” said Sergeant Gutierrez. “The wounded were taken out on medevac.”

Back at command and control, Captain Parker heard that the helicopters were on the ground with the wounded but he could not move the helicopters due to terrain and weather conditions.

“Radio transmissions would block the signal due to terrain and vertical cliffs,” he said. “Helicopters were vulnerable and there was pressure to do everything we could to get the teams out quickly.”

Fog started rolling into the valley.

“The helicopter couldn’t fly [due to altitude] and the situation called for ‘aggressive patience,'” said Captain Parker. “More than 50 percent of the U.S. forces were wounded and it was pretty grave.”

Toward the end of the fighting 40 insurgents were killed and 100 wounded.

Sergeant Rhyner was directly credited with the entire team’s survival due to his skill and poise under intense fire.

“Sergeant Rhyner is out of training less than a year and is in one of the most difficult situations” said Captain Parker. “It is an absolute testament to his character and the training these guys take. It tells me we are doing something right.”

“If it wasn’t for Zach, I wouldn’t be here,” said Sergeant Gutierrez.

Sergeant Rhyner received the Jewish Institute for National Security Affairs Grateful Nation Award and is awaiting the presentation of the Purple Heart for the injuries he suffered during the battle.

"THE YOUNG OUTDOORSMAN"

It was fortunate for John Adams that Hillsboro, Illinois, had a lot of wide-open spaces. The woods and fields outside of town became his boyhood playground. Fishing, hunting, camping and playing with his friends kept him busy throughout the year, and the many nearby lakes provided cool fun in the summer.

So it was somewhat surprising that John wasn't more upset when his parents decided to move to Florida before he started high school. Sure, he was sad to leave his friends behind in Hillsboro, but he also was filled with positive anticipation.
I've never minded change, and I was always looking for some new adventure, some new excitement.

A TWIST OF FATE

John Adams attended Milton High School, near Pensacola. He quickly became a Florida State Seminoles fan and was determined to study Forestry there. But he was disappointed when the scholarships he had hoped for were not offered. Not wanting to assume a huge student loan debt, Adams considered the military. He could go to college and have a career. And there was always the aspect of adventure. Between his uncle Dennis, a Navy Recruiter who often talked to his nephew about his experiences, and the nearby Pensacola Naval Air Station, Adams was well versed in the opportunities of the Navy. But the Navy didn't seem like the appropriate fit. As a high school senior in 1994, Adams decided to join the Marines. He set up a meeting with a Marine Corps Recruiter. But on the day of his scheduled appointment, Adams waited alone outside the Marine Corps recruiting office. The Recruiter was a no-show.

As fate would have it, an Army recruiting off was next door to the Marine Corps recruiting center. An Army Recruiter watched the eager young Adams pacing outside. He then approached Adams and gave him his card. The Recruiter never pressured him. He told Adams to go and do some research on the Army and come back if he had any questions.
In the Army, there are two people you will always remember: one is your Recruiter and the other is your Drill Sergeant.

A week later, Adams was sitting in the Army Recruiter's office. Not yet 18 years old, he would have to get his parents' written consent to join the Army as part of the Delayed Entry Program. After taking the assessment tests, the Recruiter spoke to Adams at length about the different opportunities available to him in the Army. At one point he looked at the wide-eyed young Recruit and asked, "Would you like to carry your weapon into battle or would you like your weapon to carry you?" That's when Adams knew he wanted to be part of an Armored Division, with the potential to someday command his own tank.

THE FIRST STEP IN SERVICE

Adams was sent to Basic Combat Training (BCT) at Fort Knox, Kentucky. BCT was the toughest thing he had ever done, but he welcomed the physical and mental challenge. It wasn't long before he began training on an M1 Abrams Tank. He learned how to drive it, how to load the massive gun rounds and how to shoot. He would spend most of the next decade atop or inside one of these $3.5 million technological marvels.

"I'LL SEE THE WORLD"

Adams was sent to Schweinfurt, Germany, to join the 2nd Battalion of the 64th Armor Regiment in the 3rd Infantry Division. He loved the adventure of being overseas and training with his unit. On his time off he explored the German countryside. The next few years would take him back to the States for intensive tank training in Colorado, and to Fort Knox, Kentucky, where he studied leadership and learned the value of teamwork. Proud of his gunnery skills, Adams and his tank crew registered several perfect scores during field training exercises. To Adams, there was nothing more exhilarating than firing the 120mm cannon from a 68-ton vehicle while it barreled over the range at 30 mph.
It was an overwhelming feeling to achieve several perfect scores with zero discrepancies. We were good!

TRAINED FOR PEACE, BUT READY FOR WAR

John Adams met his wife, Jodi, at a wedding in her Indiana hometown. John and Jodi married on July 15, 2000, and, shortly thereafter, Adams received orders to depart Fort Knox for Camp Casey, South Korea. He took his new bride with him on this next adventure. It was Jodi's first time on an airplane, but it certainly would not be her last. John trained in armor tactics in the rugged terrain of the Korean Peninsula, and then was selected to attend the Basic Noncommissioned Officers' Course at Fort Knox, Kentucky. While in Kentucky, the Adams' welcomed their beautiful daughter, Emma to the Army family.

Upon graduation, SSG Adams received orders to Vilseck, Germany. He settled his family into the lovely German countryside and joined his unit in Kosovo for a two-month deployment as part of a NATO peacekeeping mission. After returning from the Balkans, John received word his unit was deploying to Iraq as part of Operation Iraqi Freedom. They immediately began preparations. It was hard to leave his family, but Adams knew the mission was important and his team was well-equipped and well-prepared.
It was Valentine's Day, 2004. That's when I said goodbye to my girls. It was a tough day for all of us.

THEY LEAVE THE TANKS ALONE

In Iraq, Staff Sergeant Adams commanded his own tank. Adams' unit immediately began conducting wartime operations that included convoy escorts, search missions, main supply route overwatch and quick reaction force missions. There was always action and excitement, but as a Commander of an M1 Abrams, Adams sometimes saw it differently.
We would move into battle and oftentimes just sit there. Something happens to the enemy when they see the Abrams roll in. They just leave the tanks alone and run.

At other times, Adams conducted operations outside the formidable M1. His unit often conducted missions at night, patrolling supply routes in HMMWVs in an attempt to keep them clear of Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) and ambush points.

THE BURIED KILLER
Throughout Iraq and Afghanistan, insurgents bury IEDs on roadways and supply routes in an attempt to disrupt Coalition transportation and mobility. IEDs are the single greatest cause of casualties to Coalition forces.

IEDs can be made out of anything. A soda can, a water container, even a shoebox can be used to create explosives. Often the insurgent bomb makers used smuggled or stolen artillery ordinance. It's simple: bury the bomb in the road or near it (usually under the cover of darkness), attach a triggering device such as an alarm clock, and wait. The bombs can be detonated remotely with a cell phone. Staff Sergeant Adams and his men were constantly on the lookout for these deadly devices.

IT LOOKED LIKE HE WAS CHANGING A TIRE

On the night of October 13, 2004, Staff Sergeant Adams was in the rear HMMWV of a four-vehicle patrol on Alternate Supply Route (ASR) Bismark, a well-traveled highway near the village of Salman Pak, 30 miles south of Baghdad. It was a moonless night with only a few lights in the distant village. It had been a quiet, routine evening. As the patrol was heading back to base, Adams received a radio transmission from his Platoon Leader in the lead HMMWV, alerting him to a civilian vehicle parked on the side of the road with an individual crouched near the rear of the vehicle. "Looks like he's got a flat tire or something," said the Platoon Leader. "Check him out." Up ahead, now visible in the headlights of Adams' HMMWV, was the vehicle.
I could see the guy on the passenger side of the vehicle. He was crouched or kneeling and wearing a white dishdasha, the traditional ankle-length robe. It looked like he was changing a tire.

Adams ordered his driver to stop about 30 meters behind the vehicle. As the HMMWV rolled to a stop, Staff Sergeant Adams jumped out, his M9 Pistol drawn.

ENGAGING WITH THE ENEMY

As a Tank Commander, Adams always carried a sidearm. Shortly after he arrived in Iraq he had put an attachment on the grip of his pistol that shone a red laser beam on the target when the grip was squeezed. In the course of combat operations he had used the laser grip a number of times. It was a successful non-lethal way of "getting people's attention." Adams recalls, "When they saw the red spot on them, or on someone near them, they would usually freeze." As Adams hit the ground running, he expected that the red laser beam would unnerve the man changing the tire. Adams would then do a quick check of the car and the patrol would be on its way.

"Do not move!" he yelled, as the man squinted into the headlights, and the red spot flickered on his head. That's when Staff Sergeant Adams saw muzzle flashes. Rounds whizzed and snapped past him. He realized he was running directly into automatic weapons fire. Two figures had popped up from the front of the vehicle with their weapons blazing. The crouching man jumped up just as Adams began squeezing off rounds from his M9 Pistol. Backing toward the cover of his vehicle, Adams emptied the pistol's magazine. The man by the car fell where he had been kneeling.

Bullets pinged off the HMMWV as Adams retrieved his M4 Rifle and began returning fire. Two insurgents, firing on the run, fled into the shadows of the adjacent field. Adams' driver dismounted and engaged the insurgents. Adams radioed his Platoon Leader just as a bullet penetrated the window a few inches from Adams' head. "Exchanging fire with enemy. One AIF [Anti-Iraqi Force] down!"
It happened so fast. I honestly don't know how we didn't get hit at such close range."

Adams slowly approached the downed insurgent, his M4 Rifle at the ready. What he discovered next was a sobering reminder of the enemy's lethal capabilities.

DAISY CHAIN

Within moments the rest of the patrol returned and began suppressing enemy in the field. A cease fire was given and Adams led an eight-man patrol to search for the two enemy insurgents. After returning, Adams' men began a search of the fallen enemy, the vehicle, and the surrounding area.

The headlights from the three other vehicles in the patrol illuminated what had previously been in the shadows. Next to the car was a shovel. The vehicle's tires were fine. Adams had interrupted the emplacement of an IED. In a shallow hole lay two 130mm artillery rounds. Small wires led to a digital clock next to the bomb. But Adams noticed another set of wires attached to the clock disappearing under the soil in the direction of his HMMWV. He carefully retraced his steps and made a disturbing discovery. About 15 meters apart were two additional, freshly covered IEDs-a potentially devastating "daisy chain" of six high explosives. Adams had probably run right over the mounds when he exited the vehicle. It was clear that the insurgents were moments away from covering up the last of the massive bombs and disappearing into the night.

Staff Sergeant Adams' actions prevented the Anti-Iraqi Forces from placing a complex-and potentially devastating-remote controlled chain of IEDs. Hidden in the shallow holes were one 155mm artillery round and two 130mm artillery rounds. Also recovered from the vehicle: an AK-47 with 10 full magazines, a PKC machine gun with two hundred rounds and seven hand grenades. Adams' personal courage and calm under fire had prevented catastrophic loss. For his heroic actions, Staff Sergeant Adams was awarded the Bronze Star with Valor.

TOUGHEST JOB

Staff Sergeant Adams relishes his experience in the U.S. Army. "It has given me everything: excitement, a chance to see the world and a good life for my family." Back home in the United States, Adams and his family have found their way back to his Midwestern roots. Adams realizes that after combat in Iraq, his Army career has come full circle. Having had his weapon carry him into battle, this Bronze Star recipient is now an Army Recruiter. Like the earnest Recruiter who approached him on that fateful day in 1993, Adams provides young men and women in Indiana the same straightforward and honest explanation of the benefits to an Army career.

This is by far the toughest but most satisfying time of my career in the Army. I'm challenged every day as a Recruiter to provide the strength and character that our Army needs. The Army has given me so much. This is my time to give back.

The 115 MPH Collision: Stopped at an intersection on Thomas Road in Phoenix, Arizona, Officer Jason Schechterle’s patrol vehicle was rear-ended at highway speeds by a driver who had suffered a medical seizure behind the wheel.

 The severe impact crushed the Crown Victoria’s rear crumple zone into the fuel tank, sparking an immediate 1,000-degree gasoline fire that engulfed the passenger cabin and jammed the doors shut.

Phoenix Fire Captain Gary West was nearby when the crash occurred. Armed with only a small dry-chemical extinguisher, he fought through intense heat, forced open the mangled door frame, and pulled Schechterle from the burning cockpit with seconds to spare.

“EVIDENCE INDICATES PARTS OF THE JET BROKE OFF BEFORE IMPACT.” — Federal investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board reveal that the doomed Learjet 60 that crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, likely suffered an in-flight structural breakup at altitude, aligning with dashcam video appearing to show the aircraft plunging nose-first without its T-tail horizontal stabilizer.

“There are indications the aircraft began breaking up prior to impact. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site... We are asking anyone in the community who locates debris to contact local law enforcement immediately.”

— National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Press Briefing in Palm Beach County

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence... Mayday, mayday, we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute... We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute... We’re going to crash into the ground.”

— Cockpit transmissions broadcast over Air Traffic Control frequencies moments before impact

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties while serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safe guard and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time.

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on, south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq.

When these IEDs exploded three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles.

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices.

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance.

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush.

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist.

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris, and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience.

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

When the Civil War broke out, Mary Walker wasn't asking for permission. She was already a doctor, one of the very few women in America who could say that back in 1855. The Army told her women couldn't serve as surgeons. So she showed up anyway and worked for free.

Confederate troops captured her and accused her of being a spy. She spent four months locked up in Castle Thunder prison in Richmond before she was traded back in a prisoner exchange.

In November 1865, President Andrew Johnson awarded her the Medal of Honor.

But her story didn't end neatly. In 1917, the government tightened the rules and took the medal back from her and hundreds of others. Mary's answer? She refused to return it. She wore it every single day until she died in 1919.

It took almost 60 more years, but in 1977 President Jimmy Carter restored her medal.

To this day, she is the only woman ever to receive the Medal of Honor.

She was stubborn, fearless, and way ahead of her time. And she never once backed down.

“WE’RE GOING TO CRASH INTO THE GROUND! WE’RE OUT OF TIME!”  Chilling final cockpit recordings emerge as federal investigators identify 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha as the co-pilot aboard the doomed Learjet 60 that plunged over 32,000 feet per minute into Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

“We’re going to crash into the ground! ... We’re going to die! Holy f***, we’re out of time!”

Frenzied cockpit audio broadcast over Air Traffic Control frequencies seconds before ground impact

Key Details from the Crash Investigation
The Catastrophic Descent: Flight tracking data released by Flightradar24 indicates the twin-engine Learjet 60 (tail number N722BD) had departed South Florida en route to the Bahamas when it suddenly rolled past 60 degrees of bank and entered an uncontrolled vertical dive exceeding 32,000 feet per minute, erupting into a massive fireball upon impact in a roadway near Lantana.

Co-Pilot Identified: Officials and family members confirmed the first officer was 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha, an aspiring commercial aviator who fell in love with flying as a teenager, earning her private pilot’s license at age 17 while still attending high school before advancing through commercial multi-engine ratings.

All Nine Aboard Perished: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that both flight crew members and all seven passengers were killed instantly in the high-speed impact and resulting explosion. No ground fatalities were reported despite the crash occurring adjacent to commercial buildings.

NTSB and FAA Launching Full Probe: Specialized go-teams from the National Transportation Safety Board have secured the wreckage site to recover the cockpit voice recorder (CVR), inspect flight control surface actuators for mechanical jam or pitch runaway, and analyze engine thrust settings.

Technical Investigation Priorities
Assessing Sudden Loss of Control: Investigators are focusing on whether the high-performance business jet experienced trim runaway, structural failure, wake turbulence encounter, or an unrecoverable aerodynamic stall at cruising altitude.

Analyzing High-Altitude Flight Dynamics: The extreme reported descent rate of 32,000 FPM suggests the airframe was in a near-vertical terminal dive, pointing toward catastrophic system failure or total loss of pitch authority.

Crew Experience and Type Rating Review: The NTSB will examine pilot rest logs, aircraft maintenance records, and total turbine time in type for both flight deck crew members. 

RIP Nathalia Gadelha and the other members aboard.

Prisoners of war have tried everything to escape, but few plans were as patient — or as strange — as Benjamin Purcell's. Held in a North Vietnamese prison camp, the Army officer spent months secretly drilling tiny holes into his cell door, a little at a time, always watching for the guards. His early-warning system was a chicken he had trained to react whenever anyone approached.

On December 7, 1969, he slipped through the opening and spent nearly ten hours outside the wire — he even caught a bicycle ride toward Hanoi — before being recaptured and thrown into stocks for two weeks. He would not see freedom until 1973. He retired as a colonel, carrying one of the most remarkable escape stories of the Vietnam War: no tools, no help, just patience, nerve, and a chicken.
