“POLITICIZATION IS PUSHING TROOPS TOWARD THE EXIT.” — A national survey of service members, veterans, and military families reveals that 53% of active-duty troops say increasing political interference and partisan polarization within the armed forces are driving them to leave service early—more than double the number citing pay or benefits.

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command, and you keep politics out of the mission. For too long, political leaders have treated the military as a partisan backdrop rather than protecting the core readiness of the force.”

— Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army Veteran & Executive Director of Common Defense

Key Findings from the National Survey
Politicization Outpaces Pay and Quality of Life: According to the latest national survey conducted by Common Defense, 53% of active-duty respondents report that growing political polarization makes them want to separate sooner, while only 5% say it encourages them to stay. By comparison, just 26% cited compensation and benefits as their primary retention concern.

Bipartisan Concern Across the Ranks: Frustration over politicization crosses traditional party affiliations. Among Republican-identifying service members and veterans, 72% agree that military families are being sidelined by political agendas, and 63% state defense policies are increasingly engineered for short-term domestic political gain.

Widespread Institutional Discontent: Over 79% of surveyed troops, veterans, and military dependents feel that civilian leadership and broader society are leaving the military community behind, with 74% expressing disapproval of how Congress oversees defense affairs.

Protecting the Apolitical Tradition: The survey highlighted strong opposition to using armed forces for domestic political functions: 55% of respondents reject deploying active-duty troops to monitor civilian polling stations or participate in domestic civil policing, reaffirming the constitutional standard of an apolitical military.

Strategic Implications for Retention & Readiness
Compounding the Recruiting Crisis: As all branches battle historically challenging recruiting environments, losing experienced mid-career NCOs and junior officers over political fatigue threatens institutional knowledge, unit cohesion, and technical combat capabilities.

Erosion of Public Trust: Decades of defense polling demonstrate that public confidence in the armed forces relies directly on its strictly non-partisan status. Partisan debates over command appointments, social messaging, and foreign policy rhetoric risk undermining that foundational trust.

Mission Focus vs. Narrative Battles: Frontline leaders emphasize that unit effectiveness hinges on warfighting competency, tactical drills, and equipment readiness, warning that culture-war distractions degrade morale in operational formations.

Honoring the memory and heroism of U.S. Marine Corporal Seamus M. Davey, an elite reconnaissance scout with 2d Force Reconnaissance Company (attached to 4th Force Recon Battalion).

On October 21, 2005, during combat operations in Abu Hyatt, Al Anbar Province, Iraq, Cpl. Davey's team entered an insurgent staging house and was ambushed at point-blank range—less than ten feet away—by four armed enemy fighters.

Struck by multiple rounds, Davey collapsed to the ground. Completely disregarding his mortal wounds and personal safety, he immediately brought his weapon to bear and opened continuous suppressive fire on the gunmen. His decisive, selfless actions drew the enemy's fire away from the doorway, allowing his fellow Marines to safely withdraw from the kill zone and survive. Davey continued to engage the enemy until he succumbed to his wounds, just three days before his 26th birthday.

For his extraordinary heroism, he was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal with Combat "V" and the Purple Heart.

"Swift, Silent, Deadly." Semper Fidelis, Corporal Davey. Your brothers will never forget.

Staff Sgt. Jeffery M. Dawson earned the Distinguished Service Cross while deployed to Afghanistan with the 28th EOD Company (Airborne) in support of the U.S. Army's elite 75th Ranger Regiment.

Dawson said the mission in Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2013, was supposed to be routine.

"That mission started out the same as every mission. The IED (Improvised Explosive Device) threat was low, and it was supposed to be a quick, easy target," said Dawson. "Upon infiltration, everything changed in minutes."

During the mission at a remote enemy compound, a fleeing insurgent detonated an explosive, killing himself and the team's multi-purpose canine Jani.

Dawson then realized that his team was surrounded by IEDs.

"Being the only EOD tech on the objective, it was up to me to clear medical personnel to the wounded and clear to all other personnel to get them to safety," said Dawson.

Despite being wounded by two separate explosions, Dawson halted the mission, disarmed the improvised explosive devices, and aided in the evacuation of dead and wounded Soldiers.

Navigating the chaotic situation in limited visibility for more than two hours, Dawson exposed himself to grave danger while locating three confirmed pressure plate IEDs and an additional six suspected devices, the award citation said.

"In any situation like that, you always revert back to training and stick with what you know," said Dawson, a Coalville, Utah native who has served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Dawson said he was inspired by the dedication of his fellow Soldiers who braved the explosive-ridden battlefield to recover their fallen and wounded teammates.

"I remember looking around at all the devastation and seeing American flags draped over casualties in an effort to help keep them warm," said Dawson.

The staff sergeant said he was surprised to be put in for the medal, second only to the Medal of Honor.

"When I got back to camp, people were coming up to me and shaking my hand and hugging me telling me that they heard great things about me," said Dawson. "I kept thinking to myself that I was just doing my job

The Fort Bragg, North Carolina-based 28th EOD Company (Airborne) is part of the 192nd EOD Battalion, 52nd EOD Group, 20th CBRNE Command (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosives), the only Defense Department formation that combats global CBRNE threats.

According to 28th EOD Company Commander Capt. Taylor J. Duren, his Soldiers conduct rigorous training to stay ready to jump out of airplanes and defuse explosive devices. Duren said his Soldiers regularly serve with the 75th Ranger Regiment, the U.S. Army's premier direct-action raid force.

"(The medal) highlights the relationship we have with the 75th Ranger Regiment since they are the ones who submitted (Staff Sergeant) Dawson's Distinguished Service Cross," said Duren.

Duren said the medal demonstrates the high caliber of the Soldiers serving in his one-of-a-kind company.

"What makes us truly unique is the level of professionalism each Soldier depicts in this company," said Duren, a native of Columbia, South Carolina, who has deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.

"This award pays tribute to the level of training we put into the Soldiers hand-selected to serve in this company and their dedication to mission success," said Duren.
